name: Richard Reginald Harding
bio: Magdalen Commoner 1875-9 and an Oxford friend of Wilde's, addressed in sixteen surviving letters as 'Kitten'. The nickname was not Wilde's invention and was not private to him: it came from a music-hall song about the family's surname — 'Beg your parding, Mrs Harding, / Is my kitting in your garding?' — and his elder brother James was Puss and his sister Amy Miss Puss. The letters run from 1876 to 1879. The tenderest belong to April 1878, when Wilde was ill at Magdalen and Harding stole him flowering branches from the New Buildings: 'I heard your light quick step down the passage this morning… I can bury my face in them and dream how nice it would be to be out again. You are the nicest of kittens.' He joined the London Stock Exchange in 1895 and remained a member until his death.
bio_note: Added 2026-08-05 under the rule that friendship belongs on the map. NO CONNECTION LINE — but he is the strongest candidate for one among the people added today, and the decision is Lovelle's, not mine. WHAT WOULD SUPPORT A LINE: the April 1878 sequence, where Wilde asks a young man for flowers, is brought a basket, knows his footsteps by their sound, buries his face in the blossoms and calls him the nicest of kittens. WHAT ARGUES AGAINST: he is ill and housebound in all three, the tenderness is of the sickroom, and 'Kitten' is demonstrably not an endearment Wilde coined — it is a family nickname from a music-hall song, shared with a brother called Puss and a sister called Miss Puss (printed 15). SIXTEEN LETTERS at repo PDF 42, 43, 46, 48, 54, 55, 59, 68, 72, 79, 86, 92 (three on one page), 93 and 109. TEN have been read at the page (printed 30, 65 and 66, folios confirmed, 2026-08-05); the other ten are located, not read, and all are rendered in the session scratchpad. DATES 1857-1932, the full name and the nickname's origin are from the editors' note at printed 15, read at the rendered page 2026-08-05. 'PUSS' IS SETTLED and is NOT another name for Kitten, which was the obvious guess: the editors' note at printed 15 gives him as JAMES HARDING, Reginald's elder brother, with their sister Amy as Miss Puss; the volume's index lists all three separately, and a third letter (printed 21) settles the sex beyond doubt — 'Miss Puss has fallen in my estimation if SHE is fetched with Swan'. The grammar of the 1876 letter agrees — 'Best love to Puss. I hope he is reading hard' is written TO Kitten ABOUT a third person. The cat-naming is a family joke on the surname, not a private endearment between Wilde and Harding, which is worth knowing before anyone reads weight into it. CROFT-COOKE TESTED AND NOT SUPPORTED. Croft-Cooke (The Unrecorded Life of Oscar Wilde, 1972) writes that 'the only occasions on which one detects an alien note in his letters both to Bouncer and Kitten is when he mentions Frank Miles, and this brings us to the first of Wilde's passionate friendships with another man'. Every page in these two correspondences that mentions Frank or the Miles family has now been read at the page - repo PDF 42, 46, 47, 49, 54, 56 and 72, printed 17, 21, 22, 24, 29, 31 and 47 - and the note is not audible in any of them. Miles appears flatly and briefly: as a travelling companion ('I have been waiting for my brother who is on circuit, and for Frank Miles'), as a name in a postscript added after the signature ('I have Frank Miles with me'), as one of a party ('a delightful time in town with Frank Miles and a lot of friends'), and most often as his father, Canon Miles, the advanced Anglican whose theology Wilde argued about at Bingham. WHERE WILDE DOES SWOON IN THESE SAME LETTERS IT IS OVER WOMEN, twice in the sentence immediately following a Miles mention: the four Miles daughters ('all very pretty indeed... My heart is torn in sunder with admiration for them all'), an unnamed seventeen-year-old with 'the most perfectly beautiful face I ever saw', and Florence Balcombe, 'more lovely than ever'. This is recorded as a negative finding rather than left out. It does not show that Wilde felt nothing for Miles; it shows that these letters are not the evidence for it, and that a much-repeated secondary claim rests on pages that do not say what it says they say. COUNT CORRECTED 2026-08-05: the figure first written here was a count of PDF PAGES, not of letters - the locator deduplicated by page, and letters to one person are often printed two or three to a page. The corrected figure is a count of 'To <name>' headings in the volume. Every such correction was upward, so the unread remainder is larger than this node first claimed.

context_engagements.note: Friendship. All four letters quoted entire — they are short, and nothing in them is off the subject of the two of them.

sources.quote: Dear Kitten, Have you fallen into a well, or been mislaid anywhere that you never write to me? Or has one of your nine lives gone? Frank Miles and I came down here last week, and have had a very royal time of it sailing. … Frank has done some wonderful sunsets since he came down; he has given me some more of his drawings. … Frank has never fired off a gun in his life (and says he doesn't want to) … But on Friday we go into Connemara to a charming little fishing lodge we have in the mountains where I hope to make him land a salmon and kill a brace of grouse. … Write to me there if your claws have not been clipped. Best love to Puss. I hope he is reading hard. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, Wednesday [? 16 August 1876], Moytura House, Cong, Co. Mayo (MS Hyde) — the house Sir William Wilde built above Lough Corrib. The elisions drop topography and a query about a drawing for Harding's sister. TWO THINGS WORTH NOTING: the cat-naming runs right through it — nine lives, clipped claws, and 'Puss', who is a third friend the letters do not identify; and Frank Miles, who is on this map, is here on holiday with Wilde in 1876, three years before they shared a house.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The earliest register of the friendship — teasing, cat-named, and reproachful about silence — and Wilde and Frank Miles on holiday together in 1876.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 55; printed folio 30 confirmed on the rendered page image, read 2026-08-05.

sources.quote: My dear Boy, Thousand thanks for your letter. Half the pleasure of getting a First is to receive such delightful congratulations. … I came down here Monday and had no idea it was so lovely. A wonderful garden with such white lilies and rose walks; only that there are no serpents or apples it would be quite Paradise. The church is very fine indeed. Frank and his mother, a very good artist, have painted wonderful windows, and frescoed angels on the walls, and one of his sisters has carved the screen and altar. It is simply beautiful and everything done by themselves. These horrid red marks are strawberries, which I am eating in basketfuls, during intervals of lawn tennis, at which I am awfully good. There are four daughters, all very pretty indeed, one of them who is writing at the other side of the table quite lovely. My heart is torn in sunder with admiration for them all, and my health going, so I return to Ireland next week.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, [circa 13 July 1876], Bingham Rectory, Notts (MS Hyde) — written from THE MILES FAMILY HOME. The 'Frank' is Frank Miles, who is on this map and with whom Wilde would share two London houses; the rector was his father. The elision drops a week of London engagements. The letter is the Miles family seen admiringly and collectively — mother, sisters, windows, screen — and the note Croft-Cooke hears is not audible in it. IT RUNS ON PAST THE PAGE BREAK, and the ending is the point: having described Frank's windows and Frank's mother's frescoes, Wilde finishes on Frank's four sisters and says his heart is torn in sunder with admiration for them all.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What Harding's congratulations were worth to him, the first Miles-household letter in the correspondence, and the sisters at the end of it.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 46-47; printed folios 21 and 22 both confirmed on the rendered page images, read 2026-08-05.

sources.quote: My dear Kitten, I am very sorry to hear you did not meet the poor Bouncer Boy; see what comes of having rowdy friends fond of practical jokes. I had an awful pencil scrawl from him yesterday, written sitting on the rocks at Lundy. I hope nothing will happen to him. I had a very pleasant time in Lincolnshire … as probably Bouncer will tell you when you see him next (I wrote a full account to him). I examined schools in geography and history, sang glees, ate strawberries and argued fiercely with my poor uncle, who revenged himself on Sunday by preaching on Rome in the morning, and on humility in the evening. Both very 'nasty ones' for me.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, Wednesday [5 July 1876], Magdalen College (MS Hyde), three days after the letter to Ward printed on the same page. The elision drops the weather. Kept because it shows the triangle from Harding's side: Wilde writing to Kitten about Bouncer, and saying he has already written Bouncer a fuller account.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The three of them as a set, and Wilde's solicitude for Ward expressed to Harding.

sources.quote: Dear Boy, You are in chapel I suppose with a divine calm in your soul. The doomed one is wretched at failure – and no tea. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, [? April 1878], Magdalen College (MS Hyde) — the first of three letters printed together on this page, and the whole of it.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The register at its lightest: a note across college, imagining where he is.

sources.quote: My dear Kitten, Many thanks for your kind note. I have a childish longing for some flowers – I don't care what – only not wallflowers. If you have any spare moments and can get me a few you will be doing as benevolent an action as giving groundsel to a starving canary would be! I am very wretched and ill and as soon as possible I am to be sent away somewhere out of Oxford, so my Greats work has collapsed finally for ever. Only that Tuckwell and William are awfully kind to me I should jump into the muddy Cherwell. Ever yours … Could you steal a branch of that lovely red blossoming tree outside the New Buildings for me? I am sick at heart for want of some freshness and beauty in life.
sources.context: The second letter on the same page, Tuesday [? April 1878], quoted whole including its postscript. Wilde was ill and had been told to leave Oxford. 'William' is probably William Ward, who is also on this map.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The ask — flowers, from him specifically, because he is sick at heart for want of beauty.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 92; printed folio 65 confirmed on the rendered page image, read 2026-08-05.

sources.quote: Dear Kitten, If there is anything that could console me for being ill it is your charming basket of flowers and delightful letter. The roses have quite given me a sense of the swift beauty and light of the spring: they are most exquisite. And I heard your light quick step down the passage this morning and am awfully obliged for your theft of the pink and white blossoms. I can bury my face in them and dream how nice it would be to be out again. You are the nicest of kittens. Ever yours
sources.context: The third letter, [? April 1878], running across the page break and quoted whole. Harding had done what was asked: stolen the branch and sent a basket besides.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The tenderest thing in either Oxford correspondence, and the one that would carry a connection line if Lovelle judges it should.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 92-93; printed folios 65 and 66 both confirmed on the rendered page images, read 2026-08-05.

sources.quote: My dear Kitten, I suppose you are reading much too hard ever to write any letter now. It seems a long time since I heard from you, and as for Bouncer I have not heard anything about him for a fortnight. In his last letter he complained terribly that his mother and sisters would not let him read. I hope your people are better, and encourage your industry in every way. I have been waiting for my brother who is on circuit, and for Frank Miles who could not get away from home till we go down to Galway together. We expect them both tomorrow. I am rather tired of sea bathing and lawn tennis and shall be glad to be down for the 12th. After this rain too there will be a lot of fish up. I am just going out to bring an exquisitely pretty girl to afternoon service in the Cathedral. She is just seventeen with the most perfectly beautiful face I ever saw and not a sixpence of money. I will show you her photograph when I see you next.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, Sunday [6 August 1876], 1 Merrion Square North (MS Hyde), quoted whole - written the same day as the Todd letter to Ward, and printed on the facing page to it. The girl is almost certainly Florence Balcombe, who later married Bram Stoker. The two paragraphs are consecutive and untouched: Frank Miles as a travel arrangement, and then the most perfectly beautiful face he ever saw, which belongs to a seventeen-year-old girl.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The clearest single test of the Croft-Cooke claim, and it fails in the space of two paragraphs.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 54; printed folio 29 confirmed on the rendered page image, read 2026-08-05.

sources.quote: My dear Boy, Thanks for your letter: I had made out the facts by a careful study of the statutes going up to town, but it was comforting all the same to have it confirmed by such an authority as the Schools Clerk. I had a delightful time in town with Frank Miles and a lot of friends and came home on Friday. My mother was of course awfully astonished to hear my news and very much disgusted with the wretched stupidity of our college dons, while Mahaffy is raging! I never saw him so indignantly angry; he looks on it almost as an insult to himself. The weather is charming, Florrie more lovely than ever, and I am going
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, Tuesday [15 May 1877], 1 Merrion Square North (MS Hyde). The news is that Wilde had been fined and rusticated for returning to Oxford a month late from Greece; he later told Ricketts he was 'sent down from Oxford for being the first undergraduate to visit Olympia'. The quote breaks where the printed page does. The Florrie is Florence Balcombe. Again the pattern: Frank Miles in a subordinate clause, and the lovely thing in the sentence is a girl.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The last of the seven Miles pages, and the third time a Miles mention sits next to praise of a woman.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 72; printed folio 47 confirmed on the rendered page image, read 2026-08-05.

sources.quote: My dear Kitten, So glad to hear from you again. I have been here fishing for the last three weeks. Jack Barrow and Dick Trench are staying with me, so I find myself far from lonely, which is unfortunate as far as reading goes. … I have become an awful misanthrope however: you won't know me next term. I had two jolly letters yesterday, one from Bouncer who is quill-driving …
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, [August 1877], Illaunroe Lodge, Lough Fee (MS Hyde). The elisions drop a paragraph of salmon and sea-trout counts; the letter runs on past the printed page. 'Bouncer' is William Ward, also on this map, and the two Oxford correspondences touch here.
